description: We're a team of geoinformatics students from AGH University in Kraków who work with satellite data. Our experience covers Sentinel-1/2 radar and InSAR, GIS, Python and machine learning, including an internship at the Polish Space Agency. We want to turn NASA Earth observation data into an interactive tool people can actually use.
summary:
PlotWise is a web app that lets a dryland farmer replay the last 30 years of real weather on their own field under six crop rotations. It reads the field's crop history from satellite-based crop maps, runs a soil-water model driven by NASA POWER and gridded weather, and ranks the rotations by the farmer's own priorities: income, holding up in dry years, putting rain to work, and soil. NASA SMAP, GRACE, Landsat, ECOSTRESS and GPM IMERG show how conditions at the field have changed and where soil moisture stands today.

It answers the challenge directly: the farmer's current rotation is compared with alternatives, and every option shows why it is suggested, the evidence behind it, what it offers, what is not known and what to check locally. The model is checked against 24 years of measured yields from Kansas State University field trials.

It matters because changing a rotation is a risk a farmer lives with for years. On the High Plains, where rain covers about a third of what the air can evaporate, PlotWise shows that risk against real years before the decision is made.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

PlotWise answers one question for a dryland farmer: "Should I change my crop rotation, to what, and what do I risk in a dry year?" The farmer picks a field and moves through six pages:

- My field: the field outline, the rotation actually in use, what grew there every year since 2008, the soil and how much water it holds, days a year with bare ground, an 18-year greenness record and a surface-heat image.
- What has changed: 30-year climate trends for that place, each labelled "reliable" only when a trend test supports it, plus regional water storage.
- Rotation replay: six rotations run through every year from 1996 to 2025 on that field's soil and weather. Four sliders set the farmer's priorities (net return, holding up in dry years, putting rain to work, soil) and the ranking updates at once. Each rotation has a card: why it is suggested, the evidence, what you gain, what you risk, what we do not know, and what to check locally.
- This season: today's soil moisture as a percentile for the calendar date.
- Region: what farmers grow on 31,660 fields in 46 counties of western Kansas, and where the model agrees with them.
- How we know: the validation, the data sources and what we do not claim.

Live app: https://kub147.github.io/PlotWise/
Code: https://github.com/kub147/PlotWise

HOW IT WORKS

- Field history from space. Field outlines and the current rotation are derived from repeated crop sequences in the USDA Cropland Data Layer. The farmer does not type the rotation in.
- A soil-water engine. A daily soil-water balance runs through every crop and every fallow. Soil water capacity comes from the USDA soil survey, daily weather from gridMET and NASA POWER, crop water use from FAO-56. Yield follows from the water each crop used, with functions published by Kansas State University.
- Every rotation in every year. Each phase of each rotation is started in each year, so a rotation gets the whole run of good and bad years.
- Money as a comparison. Yield times the Kansas price of that year, minus the Kansas State budget cost, in 2025 dollars, scored against wheat-fallow on the same field.
- Priorities, not a verdict. The engine also tries 5,000 random sets of priorities and reports how often each rotation comes first. When no rotation wins under most priorities, the app says the choice is a close call.

HOW FAR TO TRUST IT

The engine was checked against yields measured year by year at the Kansas State University research station in Tribune, 1996-2020. Modelled water use explains about 61% of the year-to-year variation in sorghum yield (54% for years left out of the fit) and about 45% for wheat (13% left out), and the app says wheat is a rough estimate. The model's two lowest years for each crop are the measured crop-failure years.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A farmer or crop adviser can see a rotation decision against 30 real years, including the years the crop failed, before making it. On the High Plains, rain covers about a third of what the air can evaporate and the region is losing stored water (about 7 inches since 2002, NASA GRACE). The engine takes weather, soil and a crop table, so it can be run for any water-limited region that has a rotation trial to check it against.

WHAT WE FOUND

- The answer depends on where you farm: the gain from replacing fallow with sorghum rises from about -17 USD per acre a year in the driest counties to about +12 in the wettest.
- The growing season is warmer and the air is thirstier, but rain shows no reliable trend.
- On the same summer afternoons, bare fallow was 8 to 10 Â°F hotter at the surface than sorghum (NASA ECOSTRESS).

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, Matplotlib, Google Earth Engine API) for the data pipelines and the engine. React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet and Recharts for the web app, published with GitHub Pages. No backend: the pipelines write small files and the app reads them. The interface is in English and Polish and has a phone layout.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of forecasting, PlotWise replays the past: the farmer sees what each rotation would have done in years they remember. The rotation is read from satellite crop maps instead of being typed in. The ranking follows the farmer's values and admits when it is a close call.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty about uncertainty. Four rainfall records were compared at every field. One (NASA POWER) shows a drying trend that the other three do not, so we do not claim that rain is declining.
- Scale. Gridded weather describes the area around a field, not the field itself, and the app says so.
- Limits. The replay compares rotations and is not a profit forecast: it leaves out crop insurance, government payments, pests, disease and hail. Each card lists what to check locally.
- Plain language and US units, because the reader is a farmer.
